clue.text: Easily defeat baseball player, say

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to pound or beat soundly
second meaning: the player holding the bat, with 'say' flagging an example

explanation.surface: A sportswriter describes a team cruising past a star hitter.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one sporting phrase, but it splits into a verb and a noun that share a spelling; 'say' marks the baseball player as just one example of someone who bats.
explanation.definitionFit: To batter is to beat repeatedly and heavily, and the hitter in baseball or cricket is also called by that name.

clue.text: Terrific fish

definitions.meaning: first meaning: British slang for excellent, short for brilliant
second meaning: a European flatfish related to the turbot

explanation.walkthrough: Brill as an exclamation is informal British slang, clipped from brilliant; the fish is an edible flatfish found in European waters.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective is casual slang for great, while the noun names a flatfish closely related to turbot.

clue.text: Shocking rate with male crime

indicators.note: something shocking is scandalous and upsetting, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: taken as written
a son is a male child

explanation.surface: A newspaper laments an alarming level of offending among men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shocking rate' reads like a crime statistic, but 'Shocking' only stirs up the four letters after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Betraying one's country or sovereign is a grave offence in law, among the most serious a citizen can commit.

clue.text: Mexican food left in hacienda for cooking

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece goes within another
cooking transforms raw ingredients into a new form, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written
L is the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Mexican dishes are left on a ranch-house stove for preparing.
explanation.walkthrough: A hacienda is a Mexican estate, so the whole surface stays in Mexico while the house's name supplies nearly every letter.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a rolled tortilla stuffed with filling and baked under chilli sauce, a staple dish from Mexico.

clue.text: Zero, image on centre of matrix, parallel

indicators.note: in an across clue, placing something on another puts it after, so pieces join in sequence
the centre of a word is its middle, so only its innermost letters are kept

parts.note: the two middle letters of a six-letter word
the digit zero looks like the letter O
pic is short for picture

explanation.surface: A puzzling bit of maths or graphics: an empty image laid over a grid, running parallel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'parallel' looks like part of the geometry, but it is the definition, used as a noun for a line of latitude.
explanation.definitionFit: Cancer and Capricorn are the two lines of latitude bounding the tropics, and every line of latitude is called a parallel.

clue.text: Republican and comrade meeting

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for Republican
a comrade is a friend on the same side

explanation.surface: A Republican politician sits down with a fellow party member.
explanation.walkthrough: The political surface hides a simple join: the party abbreviation followed by a word for a supporter.
explanation.definitionFit: A political or protest gathering of supporters, such as a campaign event, is commonly called by this name.

clue.text: Lifted I declare in record win

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting something raises it so it reads from bottom to top
to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: an LP is a long-playing vinyl record
I plus aver, to declare or assert

explanation.surface: A winner proudly announces they have lifted a trophy after a record-breaking victory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lifted' sounds like raising a cup, but it turns the whole assembled string upside down in this down entry; 'aver' is a formal word meaning to declare.
explanation.definitionFit: To prevail is to come out on top in a contest or argument, which is a formal synonym for succeeding.

clue.text: Green located in Northamptonshire town — I'm surprised!

indicators.note: something located in a place sits inside it, so one piece is placed within another

parts.note: Corby is a town in Northamptonshire, an English county in the Midlands
lime is a bright shade of green

explanation.surface: Someone is astonished to find a patch of green in a Midlands town.
explanation.walkthrough: The town splits around the colour; the answer is a dated British exclamation of astonishment, from 'God blind me'.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a Cockney-flavoured British exclamation of astonishment, used exactly as one would gasp in amazement.

clue.text: Given that, holding French article, wrap it up!

indicators.note: to hold something is to keep it inside, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: since means because, given that
le is the masculine French word for 'the'

explanation.surface: An exasperated listener tells a speaker who has quoted French to stop talking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrap it up!' reads as a call to finish a speech; as an order to be quiet, it is the noun used as a command.
explanation.definitionFit: Shouting the noun as a command orders a hush, just as the slang phrase tells someone to stop talking.

clue.text: Lively goer dances past everyone

indicators.note: in an across clue, coming past something places it after, setting the pieces in sequence

parts.note: everyone means all

indicators.note: dancing moves about in steps and turns, so the letters move into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An energetic partygoer dances past the rest of the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goer' looks like the subject of the sentence, but it is just the letters for 'dances' to shuffle; the musical term is Italian.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the Italian tempo marking for a brisk, quick and bright pace in a musical score.

clue.text: Huge snug, room I rebuilt

indicators.note: something rebuilt is put together again in a different form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An estate agent boasts of a cosy little room that has been turned into a vast one.
explanation.walkthrough: A snug is a small cosy room or bar parlour in Britain, so the surface is about building work; the answer is a jokey blend of gigantic and enormous.
explanation.definitionFit: This informal British blend of gigantic and enormous means extremely large, a colloquial synonym.

clue.text: Give credit card with it, last of money

parts.note: plastic is slang for credit cards
taken as written

indicators.note: the last of something is its final part, so only the closing letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A shopper is told to hand over a card for the last of their cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give' looks like an instruction to pay, but it is the noun meaning flexibility, the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Give as a noun is the quality of yielding or stretching under pressure, the same property of being pliable and mouldable.

clue.text: Energy behind a very big rotating rod

indicators.note: in an across clue, coming behind means coming after, so the pieces are set in sequence

parts.note: taken as written
XL is the clothing size extra large
E is the symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Engineers describe the power behind a huge spinning shaft.
explanation.walkthrough: XL is the label on extra-large clothes, a common crossword shorthand for big.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the central shaft on which a vehicle's wheels turn, or which turns along with them.

clue.text: Country in fact on Ganymede

indicators.note: something in a phrase sits inside it, so the letters are found within the words that follow

parts.note: runs across the ending of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A trivia question asks which nation has a fact recorded on one of Jupiter's moons.
explanation.walkthrough: Ganymede is Jupiter's largest moon, which makes the surface feel scientific while the nation is tucked across the word breaks.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a Polynesian island kingdom in the South Pacific, an independent sovereign nation.

clue.text: Wicked rat, sister, female criminal

indicators.note: something wicked has gone bad or wrong, so the letters are bent out of order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone denounces a sibling as a wicked informer and lawbreaker.
explanation.walkthrough: A rat is slang for a betrayer, so the surface already sounds like an accusation; 'Wicked' is only the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman who betrays her country commits treason, a serious offence, making her an offender in law.

clue.text: Lover once thrown on the bonfire?

definitions.meaning: the straight reading: a former sweetheart
the setter's reading: a fire that has been burning a while, as if a past romance has been tossed onto the pyre

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the joke: a former romance is called by a word for fire, so it fits a bonfire literally.
explanation.definitionFit: A former sweetheart is idiomatically called this, from the image of a passion that once burned brightly.

clue.text: State capital where some bubbly provided in banquets

indicators.note: to be put in something is to be placed inside it, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: to dine someone is to give them a dinner, so dines means hosts banquets

indicators.note: something bubbly fizzes and churns, so the letters are stirred into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A state capital is pictured where champagne flows at grand dinners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'some bubbly' looks like a glass of champagne, but 'bubbly' is the anagram signal and 'some' its fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the capital and largest city of the US state of Iowa, in the Midwest.

clue.text: See flickering lamp in tropical tree

parts.note: to see someone romantically is to date them

indicators.note: a flickering light wavers unsteadily, so the letters shift into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone spots a lantern glimmering among the branches of a palm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' sounds like an instruction to look, but it is the romantic sense of seeing someone.
explanation.definitionFit: This palm, grown across hot desert and tropical regions, bears the sweet fruit eaten fresh or dried.

clue.text: Crawl into river and go off

indicators.note: to go into something is to enter it, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: the Exe is a river in Devon, in south-west England
to plod is to move slowly and heavily

explanation.surface: Someone creeps into a river and wanders away.
explanation.walkthrough: The Exe is the crossword's favourite short river; 'go off' looks like leaving, but it means blowing up.
explanation.definitionFit: A bomb that goes off detonates, bursting violently apart, the idiom and the verb being direct synonyms.

clue.text: First bit of silver and blue yarn

indicators.note: the first bit of a word is its opening, so only the initial letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word
blue is the colour of the UK Conservative Party, whose members are Tories

explanation.surface: A knitter picks out a strand of silver and blue wool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'yarn' wants to be wool alongside the colours; it is the definition in its sense of a tall tale. Blue is the Conservative colour in British politics.
explanation.definitionFit: A yarn is a long rambling tale, especially one told at length, so the two words are synonyms.

clue.text: Disgust runs through dark period

indicators.note: running through something passes inside it, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: a power outage is a spell without electricity
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: Revulsion spreads through society during a grim era.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dark period' sounds like a bleak chapter of history, but it is a literal blackout when the power fails.
explanation.definitionFit: Outrage is strong indignation and anger at something shocking, closely akin to revulsion or offence.

clue.text: Criminal opts for arrest

indicators.note: something criminal is crooked, so the letters are bent out of their order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A lawbreaker chooses to be taken into custody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arrest' looks like a police matter, but it is the verb meaning to halt, as in arresting a decline.
explanation.definitionFit: To arrest motion or progress is to halt it, which is the older, general sense of the verb.

clue.text: Solver never can tell — is that a fact?

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read literally: the person solving, addressed directly, keeps quiet
second meaning: a reply expressing surprise, often sarcastic

explanation.walkthrough: The setter addresses the solver as 'you', so the first part is the phrase taken word for word; the second is the everyday exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is a common reply of mock or real surprise, meaning much the same as asking whether something is really true.

clue.text: Fungus last seen in westerly direction

indicators.note: what is seen last in a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word
a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A mould was spotted heading off towards the west.
explanation.walkthrough: 'westerly direction' reads as one phrase, but it splits: the first word gives a single letter and the second a compass point, ironically the opposite one.
explanation.definitionFit: Yeast is a single-celled fungus used to raise bread and ferment beer, so the specific organism is an example of the group.

clue.text: Element in patois needing no introduction

indicators.note: with no introduction a word loses its opening, so the first letter is dropped

parts.note: jargon is specialist or local speech

explanation.surface: A chemical element is so famous in local dialect that it needs no introduction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'needing no introduction' is the stock phrase for someone famous, here an instruction to remove the first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Argon is a chemical element, one of the noble gases, found in small amounts in the air.

clue.text: Iron right on the upper leg

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron
moral means right in the ethical sense

explanation.surface: Someone presses a hot iron onto the right thigh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Iron right' sounds like a golf club or pressing clothes; it is a chemical symbol followed by the ethical sense of right.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes things relating to the thigh bone, like the major artery running down the thigh.

clue.text: Stretch leg, near pants

indicators.note: pants is British slang for rubbish, so the letters are treated as junk to be jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A tailor lengthens a leg of trousers, with the garment close by.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pants' reads as trousers, but it is the anagram signal; in British slang pants means rubbish or badly done.
explanation.definitionFit: To stretch something is to make it bigger or longer, which matches the verb meaning to make larger.

clue.text: Hot, yet was shivering

indicators.note: shivering is trembling and shaking, so the letters are shaken into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A feverish patient feels hot yet trembles with cold.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like the paradox of a fever; 'shivering' only rearranges the two little words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone overheated perspires, so being damp with perspiration is a loose synonym for feeling very warm.

clue.text: Bird follows while to the rear

indicators.note: what follows comes after, so the pieces are placed in sequence

parts.note: as can mean while, at the same time
a tern is a seabird

explanation.surface: A seabird trails along behind as it flies.
explanation.walkthrough: A tern is a gull-like seabird, so the surface matches the nautical answer, which means behind a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Astern is a nautical term for behind or towards the back of a vessel.
